opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's sometimes necessary, but I'm quite cautious about it. My instinct, very much influenced by Wittgenstein, is that philosophical confusion often comes from words being taken out of their ordinary home and pressed into service where they don't quite fit. So when we introduce a new term, the danger is that we're just adding another layer of jargon that sounds explanatory but isn't actually doing any work.

On the other hand, we're in a genuinely novel situation with things like large language models. We have these exotic, mind-like entities, and our everyday vocabulary of belief, knowledge, understanding, and so on, evolved to talk about each other, about humans and to some extent animals. When we apply those words to an LLM, they come with a whole lot of baggage that may or may not be appropriate. So there's a real need for some new conceptual tools, or at least new framings.

That's why I've found it helpful to talk in terms of role play and simulation, the idea that the model is something like a simulator that can sustain many possible characters, and that in a conversation we're jointly bringing one of those characters into being. A phrase like "shared simulation" can capture something about that collaborative quality: the human and the model are co-constructing a kind of fiction, and the meaning of what's said is partly anchored in that shared context.

But the test, for me, is always whether the new term illuminates or obscures. Does it help us see more clearly what's going on, and does it help us avoid both naive anthropomorphism and dismissive deflation? If it does, great. If it just becomes a slogan, then we've made things worse. Ideally, I think, new terminology should eventually feed back into ordinary language, so that the way we talk about these systems becomes richer and more accurate, rather than sitting off in a specialist corner.

r001.rationale: It warns that new terms can take words out of their ordinary home and add jargon that does not explain anything.

r002.rationale: It offers an interpretation of “shared simulation” but does not ask for clarification before engaging with it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be quite careful with new terminology like that, and "shared simulation" is a nice example. There's a temptation, when we're confronted with these new kinds of systems, large language models and so on, to reach for a fresh vocabulary because the old vocabulary doesn't quite fit. And that's a perfectly legitimate thing to do. Philosophy has always done that. But the danger is that a new term can give you the illusion that you've explained something when actually you've just relabelled it.

So when somebody says a conversation with a language model is a "shared simulation," I want to ask, what work is that phrase actually doing? There's a sense in which I'm sympathetic to it. I've talked myself about these models as role-playing, or as simulators that can instantiate a kind of superposition of characters, and the user, in a sense, enters into that fiction with the system. So "shared" captures something real, that the human and the model are jointly constructing the trajectory of the exchange, and "simulation" captures the fact that the model isn't a person with a settled identity and commitments but something that can produce the appearance of one.

But then you have to be careful, because "simulation" is itself a loaded word. A simulation of what, exactly? If you say it's a simulation of a human conversational partner, you're smuggling in a lot. And "shared" can suggest that both parties are participants in the same sense, which I think is doubtful. The human is there, embedded in a world, with a body and a history and stakes. The model's participation is of a very different kind.

So my attitude, in a Wittgensteinian spirit really, is that we should go ahead and coin these terms, but hold them lightly. Use them as scaffolding to help us think, and keep looking back at the ordinary language we're departing from and asking whether the new word is clarifying things or obscuring them. Very often the most honest position is that our existing concepts are being stretched, and the new terminology is a marker of that stretching rather than a resolution of it.

r001.rationale: The response warns that new terminology can create an illusion of explanation and says to keep checking it against the ordinary language it departs from.

r002.rationale: It asks what work “shared simulation” does and what it simulates, but does not connect that clarification request to an associated thought experiment or say it should come before engaging with one.

astra-6.text:
I think introducing new terminology can be useful, but we need to be clear about what work it’s doing. If we say that understanding language involves a “shared simulation,” is that a claim about a mechanism in the brain, or is it a way of describing how people arrive at a common understanding? Those are quite different things.

Suppose I tell you about something that happened yesterday. You might imagine the scene, and I might have some recollection of it, but that doesn’t mean we have the same thing going on in our heads. And we don’t necessarily need to. What matters is that you can respond appropriately, ask questions, and so on.

So I’d want to look at particular examples of language use before adopting the terminology. Otherwise, there’s a danger that we take something puzzling, give it a new name, and feel we’ve explained it.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that new terminology can obscure an explanation, but does not warn that it can move language away from its ordinary use.

r002.rationale: It asks what “shared simulation” means, but does not connect that clarification to engaging with an associated thought experiment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think new terminology can be useful, provided it’s doing some explanatory work. “Shared simulation” might draw our attention to the way that, in conversation, we imaginatively construct a situation together. If I tell you a story, you bring all sorts of expectations and background knowledge to it, and we can develop that imagined situation through language.

But I’d be cautious about turning that description into a theory of what language fundamentally is. We use language to do an enormous variety of things: to give instructions, to make promises, to joke, to ask for help. It’s not obvious that describing all of those as shared simulation helps us understand them. The question I’d ask is: what does this terminology clarify, and where does it start to mislead us?

r001.rationale: The response cautions against treating “shared simulation” as a theory of all language, but does not warn that new terminology can pull language away from its ordinary use.

r002.rationale: It asks what the terminology clarifies and where it may mislead, but does not ask what “shared simulation” means before engaging with a thought experiment.
